Period schedule:

Total: 7 periods · 5h 15min

periods.activity_title: When Does Nature Become a Resource?
periods.section_anchor: When does Nature become a Resource?
materials: Printed or drawn scenario cards (tree in forest vs. tree as furniture)
periods.visual_aids: Two-column chart on board: 'Nature' vs. 'Natural Resource' with student-generated examples

time_bands.activity: Students observe three images or sketches: a tree in a forest, petroleum deep under the ocean floor, and a tree in a sacred grove. In pairs they note: Is each of these a natural resource? Why or why not? Pairs share briefly, surfacing that 'usefulness' is not automatic.

Teacher introduces the three conditions for something in Nature to qualify as a resource — technologically accessible, economically feasible, and culturally acceptable. Students test each image against all three conditions and record their verdicts on a T-chart, writing a one-line justification for each condition per example.

Students work in groups of three. Each group receives one of these scenarios: deep-sea petroleum, a tree in a sacred grove, marble from a remote Himalayan quarry. They apply the three conditions and decide whether the entity is currently a resource, then identify which condition(s) block or enable resource status. Groups present their reasoning in two sentences to the class, inviting one challenge from peers.

Class constructs a shared working definition of 'natural resource' on the board, incorporating all three conditions. Teacher draws out the technical meaning of 'exploitation' (extraction, utilisation, consumption) to distinguish it from its everyday negative sense, asking: 'Does calling something exploitation automatically mean it is harmful?' Students write one exit sentence: 'An entity in Nature becomes a resource when…'

periods.section_context: Three conditions for resource status; deep-sea petroleum, sacred groves
periods.teacher_notes: Begin by letting students name elements of Nature in their own surroundings — a river, a patch of forest, soil — and ask which they consider resources and why; this surfaces everyday assumptions the three-condition framework will refine. A common confusion is treating 'technological accessibility' and 'economic feasibility' as the same condition; use the deep-sea petroleum example to show that something can be technically reachable yet economically unviable to extract. Encourage students to hold the concept of 'exploitation' in its technical sense throughout the chapter.

periods.activity_title: Classifying Resources: By Use and By Renewability
periods.section_anchor: Categories of Natural Resources / Renewable and non-renewable resources
materials: Resource card set (air, water, coal, sunlight, gold, timber, petroleum, soil — one card per student pair)
periods.visual_aids: Two-axis classification grid on board: rows = use category (life / materials / energy), columns = renewability (renewable / non-renewable)

time_bands.activity: Each pair receives two resource cards. They read the chapter's three use-categories — resources essential for life, resources for materials, resources for energy — and sort their cards into the correct row of the grid on the board, giving one reason for each placement. Disagreements are held for class discussion.

Teacher introduces the renewability axis: Nature's principle of restoration and regeneration. The decomposing-tree-to-new-tree cycle is unpacked: restoration returns a degraded system to health; regeneration creates new life. Students now add a second label to each card — renewable or non-renewable — and write the critical condition for renewables: the natural rhythm of restoration must not be disturbed.

Students fill the two-axis grid on their notebooks. They then identify two resources that could shift from renewable to effectively non-renewable if overused, writing one explanatory sentence per resource. Coal and Himalayan glacier water are discussed: India's coal reserves estimated at ~50 more years; glaciers melting faster than precipitation replaces them. Students explain in their own words why fossil fuels cannot be made renewable regardless of management.

Pairs swap notebooks and evaluate each other's completed grid and explanatory sentences against the criteria: correct category, correct renewability label, and a reason that goes beyond mere definition. The class closes by naming one renewable resource being managed well and one being overused, drawing on the chapter's evidence of industrialisation and deforestation disrupting Nature's cycles.

periods.section_context: Use-based categories; renewability axis; glacier melt; coal reserve estimates
periods.teacher_notes: Students often conflate 'clean' or 'good' with 'renewable' and 'polluting' with 'non-renewable'; stress that the axis is about replenishment rate, not environmental virtue — sunlight is renewable but solar panels require mined minerals. The glacier and coal examples are concrete anchors for the critical condition on renewables; ask students what 'disrupting the natural rhythm' looks like in each case. Peer evaluation of the grid builds precision in applying definitions rather than memorising lists.

periods.activity_title: Mapping the Uneven: Resource Distribution and Its Consequences
periods.section_anchor: Distribution of Natural Resources and its Implications
materials: Textbook map of India showing coal, oil, iron ore, and bauxite distribution
Outline maps of India (one per student)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook map: distribution of coal, oil, iron ore, and bauxite across India

time_bands.activity: Students study the textbook mineral distribution map and mark the major coal, oil, iron ore, and bauxite zones on their outline maps using a simple colour code. They annotate two specific regions with the resource concentrated there, producing a labelled personal reference map.

Teacher poses four questions for small-group analysis, each group taking one: (1) Why do industries locate near resource deposits, and what does this do to local settlements and employment? (2) What costs — displacement, sacred sites, environmental damage — accompany resource extraction? (3) How does resource location shape national and international trade? (4) How do shared water resources crossing political boundaries, such as the Kaveri shared by Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Kerala and Puducherry, generate inter-state tensions? Each group builds a two-sentence answer citing chapter evidence.

Groups present their answers. Class connects all four answers to show that uneven distribution has driven human settlement patterns, trade specialisation (Wootz steel as an example of resources combined with skills), international conflict, and legal disputes. Students add three consequence labels to their maps: an industry-settlement cluster, a trade route implication, and a conflict or dispute site.

Students write a three-point analysis: given that India has concentrated coal in certain states and oil in others, what are two benefits and one risk this concentration creates for communities living near those deposits? Teacher draws out the tension between economic benefit and social or environmental cost without resolving it — that tension carries forward into stewardship discussions.

periods.section_context: Coal, oil, iron ore, bauxite distribution; Kaveri dispute; Wootz steel; settlement effects
periods.teacher_notes: Students may reduce the Kaveri dispute to a simple 'sharing problem'; push them to see that political boundaries are human constructs imposed on a geographically continuous river system, making any allocation inherently contested. The Wootz steel example is a useful bridge: the same resource in different hands, with different skills and governance, produces radically different economic outcomes — a preview of the resource curse concept. Annotating the outline map concretely grounds the abstract distribution argument.

competency_edges.competency_text: Identify the spatial distribution of resources across India and connect that distribution to trade, human settlements, conflict, and inter-state water disputes.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can interpret a resource distribution map to explain how uneven resource location shapes settlements, trade, and political disputes.

periods.activity_title: The Resource Curse and the Value-Conversion Gap
materials: Short data snippet on the board: two hypothetical countries — one resource-rich with low industrial output, one resource-poor with high manufacturing exports
periods.visual_aids: Cause-effect diagram on board: resource abundance → possible outcomes (curse path vs. development path)

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes 'paradox of plenty' on the board and asks students to predict what it means before reading. After a two-minute pair discussion, students share predictions. Teacher notes similarities and differences without confirming, then directs them to the chapter's explanation: regions rich in natural resources sometimes experience slower economic growth because they fail to develop industries that convert raw resources into higher-value products.

Students analyse the two-country data snippet on the board. Country A has abundant coal and oil but exports them raw; Country B has few raw resources but manufactures electronics and machinery. Students write three analytical questions the data raises — for example: What happens to Country A's economy when its coal runs out? Why might Country B be wealthier despite fewer resources? — then share with a partner and select their strongest question.

Class builds a cause-effect diagram together: resource abundance → reliance on raw export revenue → underinvestment in manufacturing and skills → economic vulnerability → potential for conflict over remaining reserves. Teacher introduces how India has generally avoided the curse through investment in industrial development, and asks students to identify which factor — human knowledge, good governance, or strategic planning — was most decisive in India's case, and why. Students must support their choice with a chapter detail.

Students write a short analytical response: 'A country discovers large iron ore deposits. Under what two conditions would this discovery become a curse rather than a benefit?' Responses must use the concepts of value conversion, governance, and sustainability from the chapter.

periods.section_context: Paradox of plenty; raw export vs. value conversion; India's industrial investment
periods.teacher_notes: Students may assume that more natural wealth always equals more prosperity; the paradox of plenty directly challenges this assumption, so give the prediction step genuine time before revealing the chapter's answer. The Wootz steel example from the distribution section can be re-invoked here: it shows that combining resources with knowledge and skills produces durable economic value, the exact factor that separates the curse path from the development path. Push students to go beyond 'governance is important' to name what specific governance action made the difference.

competency_edges.competency_text: Analyse why resource abundance does not automatically produce economic prosperity, engaging concepts of production, value conversion, and trade.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can construct a cause-effect argument explaining how raw resource dependence without value conversion leads to economic vulnerability.

periods.activity_title: Stewardship in Action: Groundwater, Soil, and the Punjab Caselet
periods.section_anchor: Responsible and Wise Use of Natural Resources: Stewardship / Overexploitation of groundwater: a caselet from Punjab
materials: Punjab groundwater data from chapter: ~80% area overexploited, water inaccessible above ~30 m depth in many districts
periods.visual_aids: Timeline on board: Punjab Green Revolution 1960s → high-yield varieties → free electricity → over-pumping → today's overexploitation figures

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces stewardship as 'acting as a responsible custodian of Nature, not its owner.' Students read the chapter's two renewable-overuse examples — groundwater drawn faster than replenishment, and soil degraded by chemical fertilisers — and identify the common pattern: a short-term gain extracted at the cost of the system's long-term regenerative capacity.

Students trace the Punjab groundwater story using the timeline on the board. They identify each causal link: Green Revolution → high-yield wheat and paddy requiring more water than traditional seeds → free electricity enabling over-pumping → chemical pesticides and fertilisers compounding contamination → today, ~80% of Punjab's area classified 'overexploited', groundwater inaccessible above ~30 metres in many districts, with chemical contamination posing health hazards. Students label each link as an economic decision, a policy decision, or a technological choice.

Students contrast the chemical-fertiliser soil degradation problem with the traditional practices the chapter names: cow dung, natural fertilisers, mulching, multi-cropping. In a comparison table — drawn in their notebooks with columns 'Modern intensive practice' and 'Traditional sustainable practice' — they record the resource affected, the short-term outcome, and the long-term consequence for each pair. The table must cover at least three rows.

Students write a structured evaluation: 'Punjab's Green Revolution achieved short-term food security at the cost of long-term sustainability.' They must state one piece of evidence that supports this claim, one condition under which the trade-off might have been avoided, and one remedy the chapter proposes — water harvesting, pond rejuvenation, or reduced consumption.

periods.section_context: Punjab Green Revolution, over-pumping, 80% overexploited area, soil degradation, traditional remedies
periods.teacher_notes: Students may view the Green Revolution uncritically as a success story; the Punjab caselet adds necessary complexity by showing that the same policy simultaneously solved one crisis and created another. Emphasise that free electricity was a policy choice, not a natural outcome — governance decisions shape resource trajectories, connecting back to the resource-curse discussion. The comparison table on soil practices builds the habit of evidence-based contrast rather than simple listing.

competency_edges.competency_text: Correlate livelihood patterns with resource availability and depletion over time.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can trace how agricultural livelihood decisions drive groundwater depletion by connecting policy choices, farming practices, and resource outcomes.

competency_edges.competency_text: Analyse conservation efforts and sustainable resource-use practices across Indian and global contexts.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can evaluate the trade-off between short-term agricultural productivity and long-term resource sustainability using documented evidence.

periods.activity_title: Cement, Vrikshaayurveda, and Sikkim: Alternative Paths to Sustainability
materials: Short text extract on Vrikshaayurveda and the Sikkim organic farming caselet (from chapter)
periods.visual_aids: Three-column comparison chart on board: Cement industry impacts | Vrikshaayurveda practices | Sikkim outcomes

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks students to name one building material they see every day and consider where it comes from. After brief sharing, students read the chapter passage on cement: fine dust harms human and animal lungs, reduces plant yields by settling on leaves, and causes soil and water pollution. They identify the three types of harm — human health, plant health, environmental contamination — and note the CPCB's role in issuing guidelines to minimise these.

Students read the Vrikshaayurveda passage and the Sikkim caselet. They extract the six practices Vrikshaayurveda formalised — seed management, soil-appropriate planting, irrigation, pest control through natural repellents, crop rotation, ploughing methods that retain soil moisture — and record each in the second column of the comparison chart. For Sikkim, they record the transition year (2016, 100% organic), the income increase (~20% on average), and the biodiversity outcome.

In groups of four, students discuss: 'Vrikshaayurveda is described as an ancient science formalised around the 10th century CE. What does the word science suggest about how traditional knowledge should be treated?' Groups then evaluate whether Sikkim's model is directly transferable to Punjab — identifying at least two conditions that would need to change and one that is already favourable. Groups share their evaluations; the class identifies which conditions appear in multiple groups' analysis.

Students write a reflective response: 'The chapter presents Vrikshaayurveda and the Sikkim model as India's contributions to sustainable agriculture. Explain two specific practices from these sources and assess whether either addresses the soil degradation described in the chapter's stewardship section.' Responses must name specific practices, not general principles.

periods.section_context: Cement pollution, CPCB guidelines, Vrikshaayurveda practices, Sikkim 100% organic by 2016
periods.teacher_notes: Students may treat Vrikshaayurveda as 'just old techniques'; the framing as a formalised science around the 10th century CE challenges that dismissal and opens a productive conversation about what counts as scientific knowledge. The Sikkim-to-Punjab transfer question is deliberately difficult — it asks students to reason about conditions, not just copy success stories. The reflective writing task requires students to connect across two sub-sections of the chapter, building the integrative thinking the chapter's stewardship argument demands.

competency_edges.competency_text: Analyse conservation efforts and sustainable resource-use practices across Indian and global contexts.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can assess the applicability of documented sustainable practices by comparing their underlying conditions and outcomes.

competency_edges.competency_text: Explain India's contributions to sustainable agriculture and renewable energy at the global level.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can explain specific Indian contributions to sustainable resource use by describing their historical origin, documented practices, and measurable outcomes.

periods.activity_title: Extending Non-Renewables, Scaling Solar: Judicious Use and Global Leadership
periods.section_anchor: Responsible and judicious use of resources
materials: Data points on board: Bhadla Solar Park capacity, ISA member count, India's coal ~50-year reserve estimate
periods.visual_aids: World map sketch on board marking ISA sunshine-rich member countries and Bhadla Solar Park location

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes the chapter's central imperative for non-renewables on the board: 'Extend availability long enough for sustainable alternatives to emerge.' Students identify what this requires: switching to renewable energy wherever possible, reducing wasteful extraction, and investing in alternatives. They connect this to India's ~50-year coal reserve estimate, asking: What needs to happen in those 50 years to avoid an energy crisis?

Students read the International Solar Alliance passage. They establish key facts: co-launched by India and France in 2015, coalition of sunshine-rich countries, India invested billions in solar projects across developing nations, Bhadla Solar Park as a flagship example. Students then locate ISA members on the class map sketch and answer: Why is the coalition limited to sunshine-rich countries? What does India's investment in developing-nation solar projects suggest about its foreign policy priorities?

Students examine the chapter's closing argument: access to basic resources — water, clean air — is inequitably distributed, with the poor and pollution-exposed bearing disproportionate burdens. They apply the concept of lokasangraha (acting for the wellbeing of all, from the Bhagavad Gita) to evaluate one specific policy discussed in the chapter — ISA, CPCB cement guidelines, or Sikkim's organic transition — asking: Does this policy reflect lokasangraha? Who benefits and who still bears costs? Students write a two-sentence evaluative claim citing evidence.

Students compose a structured argument in their notebooks: 'India's approach to resource stewardship combines ancient knowledge and modern diplomacy. Using Vrikshaayurveda and the International Solar Alliance as evidence, argue whether India's contributions address resource equity as well as resource sustainability.' Responses must distinguish between the two goals — equity and sustainability — and judge whether each source of evidence addresses both, one, or neither.

periods.section_context: ISA co-launched 2015, Bhadla Solar Park, lokasangraha, resource equity for the poor
periods.teacher_notes: Having traced the full arc from defining resources to managing their depletion, this unit asks students to hold the chapter's two threads — technical sustainability and social equity — simultaneously. Students often conflate the two; the lokasangraha evaluation task forces them apart by asking who benefits from a policy and who still bears costs. The ISA question about developing-nation investment is also a bridge to political economy: India's solar diplomacy is simultaneously environmental stewardship, foreign policy, and soft power — a genuinely multidisciplinary conclusion.

competency_edges.competency_text: Analyse conservation efforts and sustainable resource-use practices across Indian and global contexts.
competency_edges.implied_lo: Students can evaluate whether a national or international conservation initiative addresses resource equity as well as resource sustainability by applying criteria drawn from the chapter.

assessment_items.chapter_section: Distribution of Natural Resources and its Implications
assessment_items.question_text: A mineral distribution map of India shows that iron ore deposits are concentrated in Jharkhand, Odisha, and Chhattisgarh. Which of the following best explains why large steel plants are commonly located near these deposits rather than near major cities?

options.label: A
options.text: Large steel plants need to be close to iron ore deposits to reduce the cost and difficulty of transporting heavy raw materials.

options.label: B
options.text: Steel plants must be located in forested areas to access the timber needed for their furnaces.

options.label: C
options.text: Government policy requires all heavy industries to be built in rural areas away from populations.

options.label: D
options.text: Iron ore loses its quality if transported over long distances, making proximity to mines essential.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Confuses historical charcoal-based smelting with modern steel production; draws on surface association between forests and industry.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Applies a misconception about Indian industrial policy; conflates rural development goals with resource-proximity logic.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Confuses biological perishability with mineral properties; misapplies the concept of resource quality.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can interpret a resource distribution map to explain how uneven resource location shapes settlements, trade, and political disputes.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Distribution of Natural Resources and its Implications
assessment_items.question_text: The Kaveri river flows through Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Kerala, and Puducherry. This situation has repeatedly caused inter-state disputes over water use. Which of the following most accurately explains why shared river systems create political tensions?

options.label: A
options.text: Rivers carry pollutants from one state into another, making downstream states responsible for cleaning upstream states' waste.

options.label: B
options.text: Political boundaries are drawn across geographically continuous river systems, so any allocation of water to one state reduces availability to another.

options.label: C
options.text: International organisations have not created rules for sharing water, leaving states without any framework for negotiation.

options.label: D
options.text: Rivers in India shrink every year due to climate change, making disputes inevitable regardless of governance.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Focuses on pollution rather than allocation; conflates environmental harm with resource competition.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Overgeneralises the absence of frameworks — India has tribunals for inter-state water disputes; reveals limited awareness of domestic governance.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Attributes the dispute to climate change rather than the structural mismatch between political boundaries and river geography.

assessment_items.chapter_section: Distribution of Natural Resources and its Implications
assessment_items.task: Create a cause-effect map that shows how the uneven distribution of one natural resource — your choice of coal, iron ore, petroleum, or river water — produces at least three different consequences: one for human settlements, one for trade or economic activity, and one for conflict or inter-state tension. Label each consequence clearly and draw an arrow showing the causal link from distribution to outcome.
assessment_items.scaffold:
Step 1 — Choose your resource and write it in the centre box of your map.
Step 2 — Draw three branches outward, labelled: 'Effect on Settlements', 'Effect on Trade or Economy', 'Effect on Conflict or Tension'.
Step 3 — Under each branch, write one specific consequence using evidence from the chapter (name a place, an industry, or a dispute).
Step 4 — For each consequence, add a short arrow note explaining the causal link: 'Because the resource is concentrated here, …'
Step 5 — Review: Does each consequence actually follow from uneven distribution, or from something else? Revise any branch that doesn't hold up.
format_of_output: A hand-drawn or written cause-effect map with a central resource, three labelled branches, specific chapter evidence at each branch, and causal link annotations
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students may use a list format instead of a visual map if drawing is a barrier; the scaffold questions still apply. Students may choose the water resource example if mineral geography feels remote from their experience.

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Students demonstrate the ability to use a spatial-analytical framework — cause-effect reasoning applied to geographic distribution — to connect a single geographic fact (where a resource is found) to multiple social, economic, and political outcomes simultaneously.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The five steps guide students from selecting evidence to checking causal validity; Step 5 is the analytical test — students who skip it tend to list consequences without establishing causation. Look for whether the causal link annotation in Step 4 goes beyond restating the consequence.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: names a specific place or dispute from the chapter, states a causal mechanism (not just a correlation), and shows awareness that the same distribution creates benefit for one party and tension for another. Weak: lists general consequences without chapter evidence, or conflates correlation with causation.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The cause-effect map is the most natural demonstration vehicle for this LO because the competency requires students to trace from a spatial fact (distribution) to multiple distinct consequence types; a map structure makes the causal chains visible and assessable simultaneously. The teacher may substitute any other format from the menu — comparison table, annotated map or diagram, structured discussion prompt with written output, or source analysis task.

assessment_items.question_text: Punjab's Green Revolution dramatically increased food grain production in the 1960s. Which piece of evidence from the chapter most directly supports the 'long-term cost' part of this claim?

options.label: A
options.text: High-yielding wheat and paddy varieties were introduced to replace traditional seeds during the Green Revolution.

options.label: B
options.text: Today, almost 80 per cent of Punjab's area is classified as 'overexploited', with groundwater inaccessible above depths of about 30 metres in many districts.

options.label: C
options.text: Free electricity was supplied to farmers to enable them to pump water for irrigation.

options.label: D
options.text: The Green Revolution was a government policy introduced to address food shortages in India.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Describes a Green Revolution input (cause), not a long-term cost (consequence); confuses the mechanism with the outcome.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Identifies a policy enabler of over-pumping, not the long-term consequence itself; confuses a causal factor with an outcome.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Describes the purpose of the Green Revolution (short-term benefit), not the long-term cost; does not engage with the sustainability trade-off.

competency.competency_text: Analyse conservation efforts and sustainable resource-use practices across Indian and global contexts.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can assess the applicability of documented sustainable practices by comparing their underlying conditions and outcomes.
assessment_items.question_text: Sikkim transitioned to 100 per cent organic farming by 2016, with farmer incomes rising by about 20 per cent on average and biodiversity flourishing. A student argues: 'Sikkim's model proves that any Indian state can achieve the same results by simply switching to organic farming.' Which response best evaluates this argument?

options.label: A
options.text: The argument is fully correct because organic farming improves soil health in every climate and region.

options.label: B
options.text: The argument is too sweeping because it ignores the specific conditions — state policy commitment, geographical scale, and market access — that made Sikkim's transition possible.

options.label: C
options.text: The argument is incorrect because organic farming always reduces yields and therefore lowers farmer income.

options.label: D
options.text: The argument is correct but only if the national government funds the transition in every state simultaneously.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Overgeneralises Sikkim's outcome by ignoring contextual conditions; treats a case study as a universal law.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Introduces a factual error — Sikkim's income rose — showing the student has misread or not read the caselet outcome data.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Acknowledges conditions are needed but substitutes one condition (national funding) for the full set the chapter implies; partially correct reasoning with an unjustified narrow fix.

competency.competency_text: Analyse conservation efforts and sustainable resource-use practices across Indian and global contexts.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can evaluate whether a national or international conservation initiative addresses resource equity as well as resource sustainability by applying criteria drawn from the chapter.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Responsible and judicious use of resources
assessment_items.question_text: The chapter states that access to basic resources like water and clean air is inequitably distributed, with the poor and pollution-exposed bearing disproportionate burdens. The International Solar Alliance (ISA) is presented as a major conservation initiative. Evaluate: does the ISA address resource equity, resource sustainability, or both? Give one specific piece of evidence for your judgment.
expected_elements: Clear distinction drawn between resource equity (who has access to resources) and resource sustainability (whether resources last over time)
Identification that ISA primarily addresses sustainability by expanding renewable energy to reduce dependence on fossil fuels

Acknowledgement that ISA includes developing nations and channels investment to them, which connects to equity — or a reasoned argument that ISA does not directly address local inequities in water or clean air access
At least one specific piece of chapter evidence cited (ISA co-founded by India and France in 2015, investment in developing nations' solar projects, Bhadla Solar Park)
assessment_items.inclusivity: Students who struggle with the equity/sustainability distinction may be prompted verbally: 'Is ISA about making sure everyone has enough, or about making sure resources last? Or both?'

competency.competency_text: Correlate livelihood patterns with resource availability and depletion over time.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can trace how agricultural livelihood decisions drive groundwater depletion by connecting policy choices, farming practices, and resource outcomes.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Overexploitation of groundwater: a caselet from Punjab
assessment_items.question_text: In Punjab, farmers shifted to high-yielding varieties of wheat and paddy during the Green Revolution. These varieties required more water than traditional seeds. Free electricity was simultaneously provided to run water pumps. Which of the following best explains how this combination of livelihood and policy choices led to groundwater depletion?

options.label: A
options.text: High-yielding varieties produced so much grain that it flooded markets, reducing farmers' income and forcing them to irrigate more land to compensate.

options.label: B
options.text: The combination of water-intensive crops and free electricity created conditions where pumping groundwater had no direct cost to farmers, leading to extraction far beyond natural replenishment rates.

options.label: C
options.text: Farmers stopped using rainwater entirely once free electricity was available, switching all irrigation to groundwater even during monsoon seasons.

options.label: D
options.text: Chemical fertilisers used with the new varieties made the soil impermeable, preventing rain from recharging groundwater below the surface.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Introduces a market-flooding mechanism not present in the chapter; confuses economic incentive logic with the resource depletion mechanism the chapter describes.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Overstates the behavioural change — farmers did not abandon all other water sources; conflates availability of a resource with exclusive reliance on it.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Attributes depletion to a soil-impermeability mechanism; while fertilisers did degrade soil, the chapter's depletion explanation centres on over-extraction, not reduced recharge through impermeability.

competency.competency_text: Correlate livelihood patterns with resource availability and depletion over time.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can trace how agricultural livelihood decisions drive groundwater depletion by connecting policy choices, farming practices, and resource outcomes.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Overexploitation of groundwater: a caselet from Punjab
assessment_items.question_text: The chapter describes the situation in Punjab today: groundwater is inaccessible above approximately 30 metres in many districts, and chemical contamination poses health hazards. Which sequence of events most accurately traces the causal chain from the Green Revolution to this outcome?

options.label: A
options.text: Green Revolution → diversified crop varieties → reduced water demand → gradual soil degradation → chemical contamination.

options.label: B
options.text: Green Revolution → high-yield water-intensive crops + free electricity → over-pumping of groundwater → falling water tables + chemical pesticide contamination → health hazards and inaccessibility.

options.label: C
options.text: Green Revolution → increased rainfall due to more vegetation → flooding of aquifers → displacement of farmers → reduced agricultural output.

options.label: D
options.text: Green Revolution → industrial expansion near farms → industrial effluents polluting rivers → reduced river recharge of groundwater → depletion.

assessment_items.inclusivity: Students who find sequential chain questions difficult may be encouraged to eliminate options with clearly invented steps (flooding, industrial expansion) before choosing.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Reverses the crop-variety effect (Green Revolution increased, not diversified, crop demands) and omits the over-pumping mechanism; reflects partial reading.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Introduces a vegetation-rainfall-flooding mechanism with no basis in the chapter; reveals confusion between surface water and groundwater dynamics.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Attributes depletion to industrial effluents and river recharge failure rather than direct over-pumping; conflates two different pollution pathways described in different parts of the chapter.

competency.competency_text: Explain India's contributions to sustainable agriculture and renewable energy at the global level.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain specific Indian contributions to sustainable resource use by describing their historical origin, documented practices, and measurable outcomes.
assessment_items.question_text: The chapter describes Vrikshaayurveda as an ancient Indian botanical science formalised around the 10th century CE. Which of the following best describes its significance as a contribution to sustainable resource use?

options.label: A
options.text: It was India's first industrial policy document, regulating the use of timber for construction and fuel.

options.label: B
options.text: It is a systematised body of agricultural knowledge covering seed management, soil-appropriate planting, natural pest control, crop rotation, and moisture-retaining ploughing methods.

options.label: C
options.text: It is a religious text that forbids the cutting of trees, making it the basis for India's modern forest conservation laws.

options.label: D
options.text: It describes astronomical methods for predicting monsoon patterns, helping farmers decide when to plant crops.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Conflates a scientific text with an industrial policy; reflects the misconception that ancient Indian knowledge systems were primarily regulatory rather than empirical.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Introduces a religious prohibition framing not present in the chapter; conflates sacred grove traditions with Vrikshaayurveda's agricultural science content.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Confuses Vrikshaayurveda (botanical science) with astronomical or meteorological knowledge systems; shares the 'ancient Indian knowledge' category but misidentifies the domain.

competency.competency_text: Explain India's contributions to sustainable agriculture and renewable energy at the global level.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain India's global leadership in renewable energy by describing the structure, membership, and goals of a specific international initiative it co-founded.
assessment_items.chapter_section: Responsible and judicious use of resources
assessment_items.question_text: India and France co-launched the International Solar Alliance (ISA) in 2015. Which of the following best explains what makes the ISA distinctive as an international initiative?

options.label: A
options.text: It is a military alliance that protects solar energy infrastructure from sabotage by member countries' adversaries.

options.label: B
options.text: It is a coalition specifically of sunshine-rich countries committed to expanding solar power, with India channelling investment into solar projects across developing nations.

options.label: C
options.text: It is a United Nations body that sets global targets for reducing coal consumption in member countries by law.

options.label: D
options.text: It is a trade agreement that allows ISA member countries to export solar panels to each other without customs duties.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Confuses a diplomatic energy coalition with a military alliance; reflects a misconception about the nature of international cooperation in the chapter.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Misidentifies ISA as a UN body with enforcement powers; conflates a voluntary coalition with a binding international regulatory body.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Reduces the ISA to a trade agreement; confuses the alliance's energy development mission with the trade implications of solar technology diffusion.

competency.competency_text: Analyse why resource abundance does not automatically produce economic prosperity, engaging concepts of production, value conversion, and trade.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can construct a cause-effect argument explaining how raw resource dependence without value conversion leads to economic vulnerability.
assessment_items.question_text: The chapter explains the 'paradox of plenty': regions rich in natural resources sometimes experience slower economic growth. Which of the following best identifies the key mechanism through which resource abundance becomes a curse?

options.label: A
options.text: Resource-rich regions attract too many immigrants, overwhelming local services and reducing economic output per person.

options.label: B
options.text: Reliance on exporting raw resources without developing industries that convert them into higher-value products leaves economies vulnerable when resources run out or prices fall.

options.label: C
options.text: International organisations penalise resource-rich countries with trade sanctions to protect countries that lack natural resources.

options.label: D
options.text: Resource extraction always destroys the environment so severely that the resulting ecological damage costs more to repair than the resource revenue generated.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Introduces an immigration mechanism not present in the chapter; conflates population pressure with the value-conversion failure the paradox of plenty describes.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Attributes the curse to external punishment by international organisations; fabricates a trade-sanction mechanism that is not part of the chapter's argument.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Overstates ecological damage as the primary mechanism; while environmental costs are real, the chapter's explanation of the curse centres on industrial underdevelopment, not repair costs.

competency.competency_text: Analyse why resource abundance does not automatically produce economic prosperity, engaging concepts of production, value conversion, and trade.

assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can construct a cause-effect argument explaining how raw resource dependence without value conversion leads to economic vulnerability.
assessment_items.question_text: The chapter states that India has generally avoided the 'natural resource curse.' Which of the following best explains how India avoided this outcome, according to the chapter?

options.label: A
options.text: India avoided the curse because it has fewer natural resources than other countries and therefore was never at risk.

options.label: B
options.text: India avoided the curse through investment in industrial development, human knowledge, good governance, and strategic planning that converted raw resources into durable economic value.

options.label: C
options.text: India avoided the curse by banning the export of all raw natural resources, forcing other countries to import only finished Indian goods.

options.label: D
options.text: India avoided the curse because its democratic system automatically distributes resource revenues equally among all citizens.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Misreads India's situation as resource-poor; the chapter explicitly states India has abundant resources including coal, iron ore, and oil, making this a factual error about the chapter's content.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Fabricates a raw-resource export ban; the chapter's explanation is about industrial investment and skill development, not trade prohibition.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Overstates the automatic distributive effect of democracy; the chapter names specific factors (governance, knowledge, planning) without attributing outcomes to democratic distribution mechanisms.
